lesson.title: The Restless State: Understanding Gases
lesson.summary: Gases are collections of particles in constant, random, high-speed motion with huge amounts of empty space between them, which is why they expand to fill any container and mix completely with one another.
lesson.body:
You already know from the kinetic molecular theory that particles of matter are always moving, and that the amount of motion depends on temperature. Gases are the state of matter where this motion completely wins out over the attractions between particles. In a solid, particles are locked in place by strong intermolecular forces. In a liquid, particles can slide past each other but still stay in contact. In a gas, the particles are so far apart, and moving so fast, that the forces between them are essentially negligible under ordinary conditions. Each particle travels in a straight line until it collides with another particle or with the wall of its container, then bounces off and continues in a new direction.

This picture explains every characteristic property of gases that you can observe in a lab. Gases have no fixed shape or volume because there is nothing holding a particle to a particular location; they simply spread out until they hit a wall. Gases are highly compressible because, unlike a liquid or solid, most of the volume a gas occupies is empty space, not the particles themselves. Gases mix completely and spontaneously (a process called diffusion) because there are no significant forces stopping one kind of particle from wandering through the gaps between another kind. And gases exert pressure on their container by continuously bombarding the walls with countless tiny collisions, a topic covered in detail in gas pressure and picked up again in this chapter's companion on atmospheric pressure.

It helps to get a feel for just how much empty space is really in a gas. Liquid water has a density close to 1.00 g per milliliter, and since one mole of water has a mass of about 18.0 g, one mole of liquid water occupies close to 18.0 mL. One mole of steam (water vapor) at standard temperature and pressure occupies about 22.4 L, a figure you will derive properly in the molar volume chapter later in this unit. Comparing the two: 22.4 L is 22,400 mL, and 22,400 mL divided by 18.0 mL is about 1,244. In other words, when liquid water turns to steam at STP, it expands to roughly 1,240 times its liquid volume. Almost none of that increase comes from the water molecules getting bigger; it comes entirely from the huge gaps opening up between them as thermal motion pulls them apart.

This is why gases are described with a different set of variables than solids and liquids. Instead of just mass and shape, we track pressure, volume, temperature, and the amount of substance (moles), because these four quantities are enough to completely describe the state of any gas sample. The rest of this unit builds that toolkit piece by piece: atmospheric pressure and gas pressure as ways to quantify the force gas exerts, the mole concept and temperature scales as the bookkeeping tools, and finally the ideal gas law that ties all four variables together in a single equation.
